body:
Cultural and religious significance

Garba is a Gujarati devotional and festive dance tradition particularly associated with Navaratri, the festival dedicated to the worship of Shakti.

A traditional feature of Garba is its association with an illuminated earthen vessel or a religiously significant central symbol. This connects the dance with religious devotion and collective festive participation.

Garba is not merely an entertainment activity. Its living cultural significance includes community gatherings, religious observance, music, traditional clothing, craftsmanship and the transmission of cultural knowledge.

UNESCO recognition

Garba of Gujarat was inscribed on the Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity on 6 December 2023.

The inscription took place during the 18th session of the Intergovernmental Committee for the Safeguarding of the Intangible Cultural Heritage at Kasane, Botswana.

It was approved through Decision 18.COM 8.b.32 and became India's 15th intangible cultural heritage inscription at that time.

This historical position must be distinguished from the total number of India's inscriptions at a later date.

Relevant intangible heritage domains

Garba particularly illustrates the overlapping domains of performing arts and social practices, rituals and festive events.

Associated songs and craft traditions also demonstrate its connections with oral expressions and traditional craftsmanship.

Bearer communities and transmission

The bearers of Garba include dancers, musicians, religious practitioners, craftspeople, families and community organisations.

The tradition is transmitted through participation, observation, imitation and organised learning. Both rural and urban communities contribute to its continuation.

Institutional training, community organisations and cultural programmes may supplement traditional modes of learning, but the continuing participation of practitioners remains essential.

Tourism and safeguarding

Navaratri tourism can increase demand for traditional clothing, ornaments, musical services, accommodation and local handicrafts. It can also create opportunities for cultural exchange.

Safeguarding requires attention to the devotional significance of the tradition, community participation and the economic interests of its practitioners.

Large commercial Garba events may represent legitimate contemporary adaptations. Their existence does not necessarily undermine living heritage. Problems arise when commercial activity displaces communities, misrepresents traditions or reduces opportunities for customary participation.

Garba and Dandiya Raas

Garba and Dandiya Raas are closely associated with Gujarati festivities but are not identical terms. Garba possesses a distinctive devotional association with Shakti and Navaratri. Dandiya Raas is associated with the use of paired sticks and the broader Raas tradition.

The official UNESCO inscription is specifically titled Garba of Gujarat. It should not be described as a separate inscription of Dandiya Raas.

Prelims focus

  • Official inscription name: Garba of Gujarat.
  • Inscription date: 6 December 2023.
  • List: Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity.
  • Committee session: 18th session, Kasane, Botswana.
  • Garba became India's 15th inscription at that time.
  • Trap: Garba of Gujarat is not a World Heritage Site or a separate UNESCO inscription of Dandiya Raas.

[References: UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage, Garba of Gujarat, nomination file 01962 and Decision 18.COM 8.b.32; UNESCO announcement dated 6 December 2023; Ministry of Culture, PIB announcement dated 6 December 2023; Sangeet Natak Akademi, Garba of Gujarat, consulted 26 November 2026.]

title: Garba of Gujarat as a Living Heritage Tradition

body:
Two distinct UNESCO conventions

The protection of physical heritage properties and the safeguarding of living cultural traditions operate through different but complementary international frameworks.

World Heritage Convention, 1972

The Convention Concerning the Protection of the World Cultural and Natural Heritage was adopted on 16 November 1972.

It concerns cultural and natural properties of Outstanding Universal Value, meaning significance of such exceptional importance that it extends beyond national boundaries and matters to humanity as a whole.

Its cultural properties may include monuments, groups of buildings and sites. Natural properties may include important natural areas, geological formations and habitats.

Intangible Cultural Heritage Convention, 2003

The 2003 Convention concerns cultural practices, expressions, knowledge and skills that are recognised and transmitted by the communities maintaining them.

Its principal concern is continued cultural viability, supported through safeguarding and community participation. It does not require a tradition to demonstrate Outstanding Universal Value in the same manner as a World Heritage property.

Feature1972 Convention2003 Convention
Principal subjectCultural and natural propertiesLiving cultural elements
Central emphasisProtection and conservationSafeguarding and transmission
Key considerationOutstanding Universal ValueCommunity recognition and viability
Gujarat exampleChampaner-PavagadhGarba of Gujarat
Relevant committeeWorld Heritage CommitteeIntergovernmental Committee for Safeguarding Intangible Cultural Heritage

Complementary protection

The 2 conventions are not mutually exclusive in their practical application. A sacred site may have significant physical architecture and also support living traditions.

Article 3 of the 2003 Convention clarifies that intangible heritage safeguarding does not reduce the protection available to associated properties under the 1972 Convention. It also preserves the rights and obligations of States Parties under relevant international intellectual-property and biological-resource instruments.

Example of an integrated heritage approach

Champaner-Pavagadh contains historic monuments, archaeological remains and an active pilgrimage shrine. Protecting its built heritage requires conservation of physical structures. Maintaining its living cultural significance also requires respect for customary religious practices and community participation.

Tourism infrastructure can help visitors access the landscape, while heritage interpretation can explain its religious and architectural diversity. Carrying-capacity assessment and visitor management can reduce harmful pressure on sensitive structures and natural surroundings.

These measures demonstrate that conservation, tourism management and safeguarding are complementary activities rather than interchangeable terms.

Three connected areas of living heritage

  • Pilgrimage networks: Connect sacred places, religious beliefs, communities and movement across geographical regions.
  • Cultural tourism: Creates opportunities to understand cultural heritage and support livelihoods through appropriately managed visitor activity.
  • Intangible heritage safeguarding: Enables communities to maintain and transmit cultural practices, knowledge and skills.

Successful heritage management protects places without ignoring people, supports tourism without damaging cultural resources and preserves records without neglecting the continued practice of living traditions.

Prelims focus

  • 1972 Convention: cultural and natural World Heritage properties.
  • 2003 Convention: safeguarding intangible cultural heritage.
  • Outstanding Universal Value is central to World Heritage inscription.
  • Community recognition and transmission are central to intangible heritage safeguarding.
  • Article 3 of the 2003 Convention preserves the protection of associated World Heritage properties.
  • Trap: World Heritage inscription and intangible heritage inscription are separate recognitions under different conventions.

[References: UNESCO, Convention Concerning the Protection of the World Cultural and Natural Heritage, 1972, Articles 1–4 and 11; UNESCO, Convention for the Safeguarding of the Intangible Cultural Heritage, 2003, Articles 1–3, 15–18; UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Champaner-Pavagadh Archaeological Park; UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage, Garba of Gujarat, consulted 26 November 2026.]
